Succinctly stated the facts discernible from the present complaint are that on the complaint of complainant, the present FIR under section 411/419/420/465/471 IPC was registered on 18.09.2006 against one Vineet Bhayana (Herein after referred to as the accused) and Guru Dutt (PO) for allegedly attempting to dishonestly encash seventy Kishan Vikas Patras (KVPs) of Rs.
5,000/- each, ISRA by ISRA ZAIDI ZAIDI 16:39:28 +0530 amounting approximately Rs.
3,50,000/- which was stated to be stolen property.
According to the case of the prosecution, on 18.09.2006 the accused visited the Dilshad Garden Post Office and presented the said KVPs for encashment.

On checking, the Post Office staff found that no record of these KVPs existed with them and that the numbers matched entries in the register of stolen or lost certificates; thereafter, the matter was reported to police and FIR u/s. 411/419/420/468/471/34 IPC was registered against the accused.

BRIEF REASONS FOR JUST DECISION OF THE CASE 20.
In the instant case, the accused persons have been charged for the offence under section 420/511 IPC and 103 Delhi Police Act.
It would be appropriate to reproduce the relevant sections.

These run as under:
Section 420 - Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property: Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to make, alter or destroy the whole or any part of a valuable security,
or anything which is signed or sealed, and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

Section 511 IPC - Whoever attempts to commit an offence punishable by this Code with imprisonment for life or imprisonment, or to cause such an offence to be committed, and in such attempt does any act towards the commission of the offence,
shall, where no express provision is made by this Code for the punishment of such attempt, be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for the offence,
for a term which may extend to one-half of the imprisonment for life or, as the case may be, one-half of the longest term of imprisonment ISRA by ISRA ZAIDI ZAIDI 16:46:11 +0530 provided for that offence, or with such fine as is provided for the offence, or with both.

Section 103 Delhi Police Act- Possession of property of which no satisfactory account can be given.- Whoever has in his possession or conveys in any manner, or offers for sale or pawn, anything which there I reason to believe is stolen property or property fraudulently obtained, shall if he fails to account for such possession or act to the satisfaction of the Metropolitan Magistrate, on conviction, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three months or with fine which may extend to one hundred rupees, or with the both.
21. The prosecution examined five witnesses.
PW1 Retired SI Ombir Singh deposed about execution of process under Section 82 Cr. PC against accused Gurudutt and Jasvinder Kaur.

His evidence is formal and qua Gurudutt and Jasvinder Kaur and does not substantiate the allegations against the State vs Vinit Bhayana on 5 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/74561796/
8 accused in the present case.
22.
PW2 Dharampal Sharma, the complainant, and a crucial witness, initially deposed that the accused had come to the Post Office and produced the KVPs for encashment.

However, during cross-examination by the Ld. APP for the State, he denied having made any statement under Section 161 CrPC, denied the date of the incident, and further stated that he could not identify the accused due to lapse of time.
He was also confronted by the Ld. APP for the State.

23. In cross-examination by the defence, he went on to state that he did not remember the exact date or month of the incident and even admitted that no such incident had ever happened,
explaining that this was why he did not remember the date.

His testimony oscillated significantly, at one-point PW2 deposed in his examination in chief that accused produced the KVPs and asked to encash the KVPs but at the same time, PW2 admitted in his cross examination that KVPs were not signed by the accused Vineet but by Gurudutt and could have been encashed only by Gurudutt.
He also admitted that the amount could have been encashed in cash and ISRA by ISRA ZAIDI ZAIDI 16:46:34 +0530 could have been encashed only by way of cheque that too in the name of Gurudutt.
Both these stances cannot be taken together as they are mutually destructive.
24. His testimony is silent if the accused had filled any encashment form or any receipt or any document indicating that he actually had come to encash the said amount.
No document has been relied upon by the prosecution to show that accused induced the post master to encash the said KVPs.
Also, it is not the case of the prosecution that accused Vineet Bhayana impersonated Gurudutt and dishonestly induced the postmaster to encash the said KVPs.
25. His testimony was vacillating, he stated that the accused had brought the KVPs, and at another denying the occurrence of the incident itself.
These contradictions strike at the root of the prosecution's case and render PW2 an unreliable witness.
His inability to identify the accused in court further weakens the prosecution's case.
Due to the indecisive nature of the testimony, he becomes an un reliable witness.
He resiled from his previous statement.
It is no longer res integra that sole testimony of complainant can be relied upon to convict an accused provided the same is reliable and credit-worthy.

In the case of Lallu Manjhi and Anr. v. State of Jharkhand (2003) 2 SCC 401 the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India had classified oral testimony of witnesses into three categories wholly reliable, wholly unreliable and neither wholly reliable nor wholly unreliable.

sentences.text: The testimony of PW4 appears to be wholly unreliable.
26. At this stage it is pertinent to note that the case of Rai Sandeep @ Deepu v. State (2012)8 SCC the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India had the attributes of a sterling witness.

sentences.text: "The Court held to test the quality of such a witness the status of a witness would be immaterial and what would be relevant would-be truthfulness of the statement made by such a witness.

What would be relevant would-be consistency of the statement right from the starting point till the end, namely at the time when witness made the initial statement ISRA by ISRA ZAIDI ZAIDI 16:46:43 +0530 and ultimately before the Court.

It must be natural and consistent with the case of prosecution qua the State vs Vinit Bhayana on 5 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/74561796/
9 accused.
There must not be any prevarication in the version of such a witness.

The witness should be in a position to withstand the test of cross examination of any length howsoever strenuous it may be and under no circumstance should give any room for any doubt as to the factum of occurrence, the persons involved and the sequence of it..."
27. PW2 has not deposed in line with his previous statement.
No reliance can be placed upon uncorroborated testimony of witness.
In every criminal trial, the identity of the malefactor must be established by proof beyond reasonable doubt.
PW2 has even failed to identify the accused.

Indeed,
the first duty of the prosecution is not to prove the crime but to prove the identity of the offender,
for even if the commission of the crime can be established, there can be no conviction without proof of identity of the offender beyond reasonable doubt.

Nothing adverse could be culled out from the testimony of PW4.
28.
Onus is, thus, on the prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the person facing the trial is, in fact, the same person who committed the offence.

29. The Hon'ble High Court of Delhi while dealing with the identity of the accused in the case of Ashraf vs State held as under:-
"....However, in case a witness is completely hostile with regard to identity of the accused even in his examination-in- chief and nothing could be elicited from him to show the involvement of the accused in the offence in the cross- examination by the APP, such a testimony cannot be accepted and made the basis of the conviction....."

30. PW3 SI Sunil Kumar, another witness regarding the execution of Section 82 CrPC proceedings,
admitted that he only visited one address at Gurgaon and did not ISRA by ISRA ZAIDI ZAIDI 2026.01.05 16:46:53 +0530 visit the second address mentioned in the process.
He failed to remember the name of the landlord from whom he allegedly made inquiries.
His evidence is also formal in nature and does not contribute to proving the alleged attempt to cheat.
31. PW4 Retired SI Mahender Pal is the formal witness who registered the FIR on the basis of the tehrir and his evidence remains procedural.

PW5 Retired ACP Satyajeet Sarin, who conducted the investigation, deposed regarding seizure of KVPs and certain documents from the residence and office of the accused, and about raids conducted at the alleged addresses of the co-accused.
However, he admitted that no public witness was joined at any stage, gave no explanation for absence of independent witnesses, and conceded that no material was found linking the alleged co-accused.

32. To constitute an offence under section 420 IPC, there should not only be cheating, but as a consequence of such cheating, the accused should have dishonestly induced the person deceived (i)
to deliver any property to any person,or (ii) to make, alter or destroy wholly or in part a valuable security or anything signed or sealed and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security as it was held in the case by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Mohd. Ibrahim v.

sentences.text: particularly stressing the requirement of mens rea (dishonest intention) at the time of the alleged act in order to attract section 420 IPC but in the present case it has not been proven by the prosecution that accused came to encash the said KVPs or he induced the said postmaster to encash the said KVPs or that he impersonated himself as Gurudutt and asked to encash the said KVPs or that he had a dishonest intention.
33. The alleged recoveries do not demonstrate that the accused had knowledge that the KVPs were stolen nor do they establish any dishonest intention required for an offence under Section 420 IPC.
The investigating officer also admitted that nothing else was recovered from the accused apart from what was already documented in the seizure memo handed over to him.
ISRA   ZAIDI
34. The alleged lost/stolen register was produced, but no FIR or complaint regarding theft of the stolen article was produced.
Also, any official from Assam Post office was examined to established that fact they were stolen property.
It was not proven by the prosecution that the property in question was lost or stolen.

It cannot be surfaced that accused had reason to believe that the said property in question was a stolen property to sustain the charges under section 103 of Delhi Police Act,1978.
35.

To sustain a conviction for attempt to cheat U/s. 420/511 IPC, the prosecution must establish that the accused knowingly and dishonestly attempted to induce the Post Office to deliver property by presenting stolen KVPs.

The only witness capable of proving such attempt, his testimony (PW2)
is riddled with contradictions material in nature.
There was no preparation to get the said amount encashed.
No form was filed for the encashment of the said KVPs.
He has denied the occurrence of the incident, denied his police statement, and failed to identify the accused in court.
His testimony is wholly unreliable and cannot be the sole basis for conviction.
36. The remaining witnesses are either formal or have not produced any evidence establishing the accused's knowledge or dishonest intention.
Having considered the entire evidence, this Court finds that the prosecution has failed to prove the essential ingredients of Sections 420/511 IPC.
The investigation suffers from serious deficiencies including absence of public witnesses, and lack of proof connecting the accused to the original dacoity.
In criminal law, the prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, and if there is even a single reasonable doubt, the accused is entitled to acquittal.
37. It is an adage that law works on the wheels of evidence.
Every criminal trial is a journey of discovering and unfolding the truth.
But in the present case no sufficient evidence is there on record to warrant the conviction of the accused person.

In the case of Prem Singh Yadav Vs. CBI 178 (2011)
DLT 529 it was held that where it is possible to have both views one in favor of prosecution and one in favor of accused, the later one should prevail.
